frontend.prompt:
Implementation tasks for frontend (synchronized with backend changes):

1) Surface-level contract
- The API will start returning a nullable top-level field deleted_at on resource representations (single and list item objects). deleted_at is either null or an RFC 3339 UTC timestamp (e.g. 2023-05-01T15:30:00Z).
- The DELETE API will no longer remove rows; it will set deleted_at to the UTC RFC 3339 timestamp on first successful delete. Subsequent DELETE attempts on an already-deleted resource will return 404 (not found) if the client is authorized; unauthorized attempts must still return 403.
- List endpoints and count must exclude resources with deleted_at != null. GET and PUT on a deleted resource return 404 (unless the request is unauthorized, in which case it returns 403 as before).

Note: Do not assume any change to existing permission model, status codes, or the exact text of success responses for the first deletion — preserve whatever status code and response body the DELETE returned before this change.

2) UI behavior changes
- Listing pages, tables, counts:
  - Assume the backend excludes deleted items and count excludes them. Do not perform client-side filtering based on deleted_at; rely on API responses for authoritative list and count.
  - If frontend has local caches or optimistic UI that could show a deleted item after server move, remove the item from caches when the server indicates deletion (successful first-delete response) or when a fetch/PUT returns 404.
- Delete action flow:
  - Keep the existing permission checks on the frontend unchanged (do not change whether delete controls are visible/enabled).
  - On successful DELETE (first deletion) preserve existing UX: keep the same success toast/notice, redirect, or refresh behavior already implemented. Do not invent or change the success message text or codepaths — simply continue to show the same success handling as before.
  - If the DELETE returns 404 (resource already deleted), handle consistent with other server 404 flows used in the app (for example, show the existing Not Found UI/modal or toast). Do not convert 404 to a permission error.
  - If the DELETE returns 403, keep the existing permission-denied UX (e.g. show existing permission error message/modal).
- GET/PUT flows:
  - If a GET or PUT returns 404, treat it as Not Found and use the same Not Found handling as other 404s in the app (do not treat it as a permission error).
  - If a GET or PUT returns 403, preserve existing permission-denied handling.
  - For PUT, if the save fails with 404, remove the item from local lists/caches and show Not Found. If the save fails with 403, show permission denied and do not remove the item from local cache.
- Create/new resource flows:
  - Do not send a deleted_at field in create requests. If the client model includes deleted_at by default, ensure it is omitted or set explicitly to null in the request payload so backend will persist it as null.

3) Client model and serialization
- Update any client-side resource models/interfaces to include deleted_at: string | null (RFC 3339 UTC string or null). Use it only for diagnostics; do not change list inclusion logic — rely on server.
- When receiving resources from the API, accept deleted_at being null or an RFC3339 timestamp. If your app uses date objects, parse deleted_at into a UTC date type where needed for display or debugging, but avoid altering list inclusion based on it.

4) Cache and optimistic updates
- When user deletes a resource and server returns success (first delete), update local caches/state to remove the item and decrement any displayed counts. If server returns 404 for a delete, also remove the item from caches and decrement counts to re-sync with server.
- If an item in cache is stale and a subsequent GET returns 404, remove it from cache and update lists/counts.

5) Error handling and user messages
- Map 403 and 404 to the app’s existing handlers for permission denied and not found, respectively. Do not invent new wording or replace existing permission/error dialogs.
- For repeated-delete (server 404 when authorized), show Not Found UI consistent with other 404 responses.

6) Tests and acceptance criteria (frontend)
- Automated unit/e2e tests must cover:
  - Listing page shows the server-provided list and count; when server excludes deleted entries, UI shows no deleted entries.
  - Create request does not send deleted_at or sends null; newly created resource appears in list and its deleted_at is null in subsequent GET responses.
  - Delete sequence when authorized and resource not deleted: server returns success -> UI shows the same existing success behavior -> resource removed from list and count updated.
  - Delete sequence when authorized and resource already deleted: server returns 404 -> UI shows Not Found handling; resource removed from list if present.
  - Delete attempt when unauthorized: server returns 403 -> UI shows existing permission-denied handling; resource remains in list if it exists.
  - GET/PUT of a deleted resource: server returns 404 -> UI uses Not Found handling; 403 remains permission handling.
- Add integration/e2e tests that simulate server responses (including 403/404) to verify UI behavior and cache updates.

7) Deployment notes
- Coordinate deploy order: backend must be deployed with database migration first and API behavior in place before enabling any frontend changes that assume deleted items are excluded. If the frontend is rolled out earlier, it must tolerate deleted_at appearing in payloads and 404 behavior.
- If you cannot guarantee deployment order, keep frontend tolerant: accept nullable deleted_at on responses and handle 404/403 as described.

8) Do not change
- Do not change existing permission model or whether a control is visible/usable. Do not change the first-delete success response’s status code/body. Do not invent new server-side error codes or messages.

Deliverables for frontend PRs:
- Code changes to model (deleted_at: string|null), request/response handling, delete handler, list refresh and cache invalidation logic.
- Unit tests and e2e tests covering the acceptance criteria above.
- Short README or PR description documenting required coordinated backend deployment order and the assumptions about the API behavior (deleted_at field semantics and 404/403 ordering).

backend.prompt:
Implementation tasks for backend (synchronized with frontend changes):

Scope and explicit contracts (do not assume beyond this):
- Add a nullable deleted_at column to the resource table; new rows must have deleted_at = NULL.
- DELETE endpoint must perform a soft delete by setting deleted_at to the current UTC time formatted/stored so it can be serialized as an RFC 3339 UTC timestamp (e.g. 2023-05-01T15:30:00Z). The first authorized DELETE should succeed and return the exact same status code and response body the current DELETE returned prior to this change. Subsequent authorized DELETEs on the same resource must return 404.
- GET and PUT on a resource that has deleted_at != NULL must return 404 if the caller is authorized; however, authorization checks remain primary: if the caller is not authorized to perform the attempted operation on the resource, return 403 and do not return 404 instead.
- List endpoints and count must exclude records with deleted_at != NULL.
- All public resource serialization must include a nullable deleted_at field.

Implementation steps
1) Database migration
  - Add column: ALTER TABLE resource ADD COLUMN deleted_at TIMESTAMPTZ NULL; (or the appropriate type in your DB/ORM). Default should be NULL for new rows.
  - Backfill: run an update to set deleted_at = NULL for existing rows if needed (most DBs will default to NULL automatically). Example SQL: UPDATE resource SET deleted_at = NULL WHERE deleted_at IS NULL; (no-op but makes intent explicit).
  - Ensure the column is nullable and has no non-null constraint.
  - If using soft-delete index or constraints are desired, create appropriate indexes on deleted_at to optimize WHERE deleted_at IS NULL queries.

2) Model/ORM updates
  - Add deleted_at: DateTime? / nullable timestamp field to the resource model.
  - Ensure create/new record code does not set deleted_at (ORM default is null). If any code constructs resources with deleted_at present, change it to omit or set null explicitly.

3) API controller/handler changes
  - Common pattern for handlers that operate on a single resource (GET, PUT, DELETE):
    a) Load the resource from DB including deleted_at.
    b) Run authorization check using the loaded resource and the same logic as currently used.
       - If unauthorized, return 403 immediately.
    c) After authorization succeeds, check resource.deleted_at:
       - If deleted_at != NULL: for GET/PUT/DELETE, return 404 (Not Found).
       - If deleted_at == NULL: proceed.
  - DELETE handler specific:
    - After step (a)-(c) and confirming resource.deleted_at == NULL and user is authorized, set resource.deleted_at = current UTC timestamp.
      - Use DB/server UTC time and persist as timestamptz (or equivalent). On serialization return an RFC 3339 UTC formatted string (Z suffix). Implementation may store as timestamptz and serialize with timezone set to Z.
    - Save/commit transaction.
    - Return the same status code and response body as the pre-change DELETE behavior; preserve headers, location, etc. (Do not invent a new success payload.)
    - If trying to DELETE and the resource was already deleted (deleted_at != NULL) and user is authorized, return 404.
  - GET handler:
    - After authorization, if deleted_at != NULL -> return 404.
  - PUT handler:
    - After authorization, if deleted_at != NULL -> return 404. Otherwise permit update as before.

4) List and count endpoints
  - Apply the same filter in all list queries: WHERE deleted_at IS NULL.
  - Ensure the count uses the same filter so counts reflect only non-deleted rows.
  - If using multiple list endpoints or scopes, update each to exclude deleted rows.
  - Add tests for queries that they include the deleted_at IS NULL predicate.

5) Serialization
  - Add deleted_at to the public resource representation as a nullable field. When deleted_at is NULL, return JSON null; when not null, serialize as RFC 3339 UTC timestamp string with Z offset.
  - Ensure the field is present in single-resource GET responses and each list item in list responses.

6) Time format and storage
  - Store timestamps as timezone-aware timestamps in the DB (e.g., timestamptz). Use server UTC time for the value; do not use local server timezone.
  - When serializing, format the timestamp as RFC 3339 with Z (UTC) or produce an equivalent RFC 3339 string including an explicit +00:00 offset. Prefer canonical Z for clarity (e.g., 2023-05-01T15:30:00Z).

7) Authorization ordering and examples
  - Important ordering: always perform authorization checks before deciding to return 404 for deleted resources. This guarantees that users without permission still get 403 even if the resource is deleted. Example flow for each request:
    - Fetch resource (including deleted_at).
    - If it does not exist at all in DB (row not found) -> return 404 as before.
    - If exists -> run authorization check -> if unauthorized -> return 403.
    - If authorized -> if resource.deleted_at != NULL -> return 404 for GET/PUT/DELETE (DELETE for repeated delete).
    - If authorized and resource.deleted_at == NULL -> proceed normally (for DELETE: set deleted_at to now and return existing success response).

8) Tests and acceptance criteria (backend)
  - Unit and integration tests must assert:
    - Migration adds deleted_at column, new rows have deleted_at == NULL.
    - Backfilled/legacy rows have deleted_at == NULL after migration.
    - List endpoints and count exclude rows with deleted_at != NULL.
    - GET/PUT of a resource with deleted_at != NULL returns 404 if the caller is authorized.
    - Authorization check is performed before deleted check: if an unauthorized caller attempts operations on an existing (deleted or not) resource, it returns 403.
    - DELETE flow:
      - Authorized and deleted_at == NULL -> deleted_at set to current UTC timestamp and response equals pre-change DELETE success (status and body). Test must compare the response to previously recorded expected status/body.
      - Authorized and deleted_at != NULL -> DELETE returns 404.
      - Unauthorized -> DELETE returns 403 (regardless of deleted_at state).
    - Time serialization correctness: when resource.deleted_at is set, serialized output uses RFC 3339 UTC format.

9) Backwards compatibility and deployment
  - Deploy DB migration first (or in the same release that is run before handlers rely on the column). Ensure code handles the presence of the column even if some instances are not yet deployed.
  - Ensure old clients that do not expect deleted_at continue to function (deleted_at is an additive nullable field).
  - Coordinate with frontend: frontend must be updated to accept deleted_at and handle 404/403 as described. If you cannot deploy frontend immediately, the backend changes are safe because deleted_at is nullable and existing success responses remain unchanged on first delete.

10) Logging and auditing
  - Log soft-delete events similar to previous delete logs, including user id, resource id, and timestamp. Keep the same logging semantics as prior hard delete events if logs existed.
  - If existing audit trails referenced deletion previously, update them to record soft delete events equivalently.

Deliverables for backend PRs:
- Migration script that adds nullable deleted_at column and any necessary indexes.
- Model/schema changes and DB mapping updates.
- API controller/handler changes for GET, PUT, DELETE, list and count as described.
- Serialization changes to include deleted_at in resource responses.
- Unit and integration tests covering all acceptance criteria (including authorization ordering and repeat-delete behavior).
- Short deployment note listing required deploy order and compatibility considerations.

Do not change:
- Do not alter the existing authorization model or visibility rules.
- Do not invent new error response codes or change the first-delete success response contents/status code. If the exact first-delete response body must be tested, capture the existing response in tests and assert equality after the change.
